A.explanation: This results from multiplying $10 \text{ J}$ by $0.0050 \text{ m}$ instead of dividing work done by displacement.

B.explanation: This is far too small because it does not account for the very small $5.0 \text{ mm}$ stopping distance for $10 \text{ J}$ of energy.

C.explanation: This underestimates the force by using too large a distance, equivalent to stopping in about $0.20 \text{ m}$ rather than $0.0050 \text{ m}$.

D.explanation: Work done $F \times d$ equals the $10 \text{ J}$ lost, so $F = 10 / 0.0050 = 2000 \text{ N}$.

hints: Notice the $10 \text{ J}$ of kinetic energy is all used to do work pushing the nail a distance of $5.0 \text{ mm}$ into the plank.
Connect energy loss to work done by the average resistive force using $W = Fd$ with force along the $5.0 \text{ mm}$ displacement.
Convert $5.0 \text{ mm}$ to $0.0050 \text{ m}$ and divide $10 \text{ J}$ by this small distance to estimate the average force.
walkthrough: Identify the useful data: initial kinetic energy $10 \text{ J}$ becomes $0$ at rest, and displacement of the nail is $d = 5.0 \text{ mm}$.
State the governing rule: work done by the average force on the nail equals energy transferred, so $W = Fd = 10 \text{ J}$.
Convert distance to SI units: $d = 5.0 \text{ mm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 0.0050 \text{ m}$.
Rearrange for average force and substitute with units: $F = W/d = 10 \text{ J} / 0.0050 \text{ m} = 2000 \text{ N}$.
Check units and size: $\text{J m}^{-1} = \text{N}$, and a large force is expected because $10 \text{ J}$ is dissipated over only a few millimetres. This is option D
